newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Markets stable on smooth Indonesian campaign start.
newsitem.headline: Markets stable on smooth Indonesian campaign start.

text.p: Indonesia's financial markets stabilised on Monday after an attack of nerves last week as the country's campaign for the May 29 general elections got off to a smooth start.
The rupiah, which tumbled 15 points at one point last week, firmed against the dollar in morning trade, rising to 2,430 where dealers expected it to be well supported after opening at 2,436.
The stock market composite index also rose more than two points to 654.65 by mid-morning, mainly on buying by local speculators as foreign investors tended to remain sidelined.
The campaign by the country's three parties that are legally permitted to contest the elections opened on Sunday, with reports of only very minor incidents.

The ruling Golkar is seeking to push its percentage of votes above the 70 percent mark after winning 68 percent in the last elections in 1992. It was campaigning on Monday in Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and the adjacent Nusa-Tenggara islands.

The Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), badly split since its leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by government-backed rebels last year, was campaigning on the main island of Java and the remote Muluks and Irian Jaya. It won 15 percent of the vote in 1992.

The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), which on Monday accused the state broadcaster of pro-Golkar bias, was campaigning in Kalimantan on Borneo island and Sulawesi in a bid to boost its take from the 17 percent won in 1992.

Nearly 125 million voters in the world's fourth most populous nation are eligible to cast ballots for the 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are alloted to the military, which does not vote.
Juwono Sudarsono, professor of politics at the University of Indonesia, said the campaign was so far quiet.
"It seems to be fairly muted at the moment," he told Reuters.

He said the calm start could be attributed to some extent to Megawati's appeal to her supporters to exercise restraint and keep out of the campaign. "It seems it augurs well for the moment," Sudarsono added.
Brokers expected thin volume and possible volatility on the stock market, but anticipated a strong surge in prices after the elections.

"We think that volume will continue to be thin, which leads to some volatility, and that the market will be pretty directionless up to the elections," Felix D'Sousa, head of research at PT Peregrine Sewu Securities, told Reuters.

"But we think that after the elections, the focus will swing back to the very well managed, steady economy, and people will see very strong corporate earnings growth coming through. I think the market will perform very strongly," he said.
He predicted the Jakarta composite index would be around the 700 level by the end of June, and agreed with other stock analysts that it should reach between 750 and 800 points by the end of the year.
